title: How climate change is reshaping Africa's malaria risk
facts: The World Health Organization African Region accounts for approximately 95% of global malaria cases and deaths.
Nigeria accounts for 31.9% of all malaria deaths in the WHO African Region.
The Democratic Republic of Congo accounts for 11.7% of malaria deaths in the WHO African Region.
Niger accounts for 6.1% of malaria deaths in the WHO African Region.
Children under five years old account for approximately 76% of malaria deaths in the WHO African Region.
The Plasmodium falciparum parasite causes 95% of malaria infections in Africa.
Malaria is transmitted to humans through bites from infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
A study in The Lancet found the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine reduced all-cause child mortality by 13.2% in Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi.
A Nature study showed malaria transmission by mosquitoes peaks at temperatures around 25 degrees Celsius.
Malaria transmission decreases significantly when temperatures fall below 16 degrees or exceed 34 degrees Celsius.
Rising temperatures are increasing malaria transmission suitability in southern Africa and the East African highlands.
Olugbenga Mokuolu is a professor of pediatrics at Nigeria's University of Ilorin.
Olugbenga Mokuolu serves as an advisor on malaria elimination to the Nigerian Minister of Health.
Olumide Idowu is the founder of the International Climate Change Development Initiative.
The World Health Organization reported in April 2025 that over half of surveyed malaria-endemic nations experienced service disruptions.
